chapter.title: Reading a real one, start to finish

cards.body:
A published balance sheet is the house photo, but taken by an estate agent: every room listed, plus the loft, the garage and the shed. **The order is always the same**: what it owns on top, fast things first, then what it owes, then what is left for the owners.

The footnotes are the small print on the back of the photo. That is where the odd rooms get explained.
cards.simpler: A company's published balance sheet is like a photo of a house taken by an estate agent. Every room is listed, even the loft, the garage and the shed. **The order is always the same.** First comes what the company owns, with cash and quick-to-sell things at the top. Then what it owes. Then what is left for the owners. The footnotes are the small print on the back of the photo. That is where the odd rooms get explained.

cards.prompt: You open a listed company's annual report and find the balance sheet. It runs over 2 pages and 40 lines. Where do you start?

options.text: The three totals: total assets, total liabilities, total equity. Check that assets equal the other two added together.
The biggest number on the page, whatever it is.
The first footnote, since that is where the secrets are.

whyNot.b: That's a headline, not a reading: the biggest number is nearly always total assets anyway, and you need to see what it is made of.
whyNot.c: That's the small print for one line. Read the lines first, then open the note for the one that puzzles you.

cards.reteach: Think of the house photo. Before you look at any room, you check the frame: everything owned on one side, owed plus owners' share on the other, same number. Three totals, one check, then you walk the rooms.

cards.title: Walk the rooms in order
cards.body:
Every listed company lays the sheet out the same way. Assets first, starting with cash and ending with buildings and brands. Then liabilities, soonest due first. Then equity. Two columns of numbers, this year and last year, so you can see what moved.

**Read it top to bottom and say each line in plain words.** *Trade receivables* is customers who have not paid yet. *Inventories* is stock on shelves. *Borrowings* is loans. A small number beside a line points to a footnote that says what the line is made of.

Odd items will appear. *Goodwill* is the extra paid when buying another company. *Deferred tax* is tax owed later. Translate, then move on.
cards.simpler: Every listed company lays the sheet out the same way. What it owns comes first, from cash down to buildings. Then what it owes, soonest bills first. Then what is left for the owners. **Read it top to bottom and say each line in plain words.** Trade receivables means customers who have not paid yet. Inventories means stock on shelves. Borrowings means loans. Odd items like goodwill will appear. A small number beside a line points to a footnote that explains it.

cards.title: Harbour Bikes, 31 March
cards.body:
Take an invented shop, Harbour Bikes, on 31 March. Cash 40,000. Customers owe it 180,000. Stock 90,000. Shop and tools 210,000. Total assets 520,000.

Supplier bills 70,000, a bank loan due within the year 150,000, a long-term loan 100,000. Liabilities 320,000, so equity is 200,000, and 520,000 equals 320,000 plus 200,000. **The sheet balances.** It also has 150,000 of debt due this year and 40,000 of cash to pay it with. The sheet balances. The owner may not.
cards.simpler: Picture an invented shop, Harbour Bikes, on 31 March. Cash is 40,000. Customers owe it 180,000. Stock is 90,000. Shop and tools are 210,000. It owns 520,000 in total. It owes suppliers 70,000, a bank loan due this year of 150,000, and a long-term loan of 100,000. That is 320,000 owed, leaving 200,000 for the owner. **The sheet balances.** But 150,000 is due this year, with only 40,000 of cash to pay it. The sheet balances. The owner may not.

cards.prompt: Reading Harbour Bikes, a friend says 'it balances, so it is fine.' Which line should make you pause?

options.text: Shop and tools at 210,000: too much money tied up in the building.
The 150,000 loan due this year, next to 40,000 of cash.
Equity of 200,000: the owners are taking too much.

whyNot.a: That's a slow asset, and slow assets are normal for a shop that has a shop. The question is what is due soon and what can pay it.
whyNot.c: That's the owners' share, and a bigger one is a cushion, not a worry. The pressure sits on the owe side.

cards.reteach: Balancing is arithmetic. Every sheet balances, including the sheets of companies that go bust the next week. The health check is a pairing: debt due within 12 months next to the cash that could pay it.

cards.title: The three warning signs
cards.body:
Once you have walked the lines, look for three pairs.

**Sign one: short-term debt bigger than cash.** Loans due within 12 months against cash. If the debt is 2 times the cash or more, ask how the gap gets paid. Sign two: a big pile of customer bills. Receivables far bigger than cash, or growing faster than sales, means the company is selling but not collecting. Sign three: profit kept, cash not. Retained earnings climbing year on year while cash sits flat or falls. Profit is on paper. Rent is paid in cash.

Compare the two years' columns for each pair. One year is a photo. Two years is a direction.
cards.simpler: Once you have read the lines, look for three pairs. **Sign one: short-term debt bigger than cash.** Loans due within a year at twice the cash or more means asking how the gap gets paid. Sign two: customers owe far more than the cash held, or the pile grows faster than sales. That means selling but not collecting. Sign three: kept profit climbs each year while cash stays flat or falls. Compare both years. One year is a photo, two years is a direction.

cards.body: Priya read a listed retailer's balance sheet and stopped at the first page, relieved: assets 2 billion, liabilities 1.2 billion, plenty left. She never opened the note on borrowings, where 900 million of that 1.2 billion was due inside 12 months, against 150 million of cash. **The totals said it balanced. The note said it was in trouble.** Spot it in yourself: if you have not read one footnote, you have read the frame, not the house.
cards.simpler: Priya read a big shop chain's balance sheet and stopped at the first page, relieved. It owned 2 billion and owed 1.2 billion, so plenty was left. She never opened the note on borrowings. It showed 900 million of that 1.2 billion was due within 12 months, against only 150 million of cash. **The totals said it balanced. The note said it was in trouble.** If you have not read one footnote, you have seen the frame, not the house.

cards.prompt: Two years of the same company. Retained earnings went from 300,000 to 420,000. Cash went from 95,000 to 30,000. Receivables went from 110,000 to 260,000. Which warning signs are showing?

options.text: Only sign one: short-term debt bigger than cash.
Signs two and three: customer bills piling up, and profit kept while cash fell.
None. Equity grew, so the company is healthier.

whyNot.a: That's the pairing of loans due soon with cash, and no loan line was given here. The lines you have are receivables, retained earnings and cash.
whyNot.c: That's the equity line on its own. Retained earnings rising while cash falls is sign three: the profit went into unpaid customer bills, not the bank.

cards.reteach: Three signs, three pairs. Short-term debt against cash. Customer bills against cash. Profit kept against cash. Each asks the same question in a different voice: can it actually pay?

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
A real balance sheet is the same house photo with more rooms, so check the three totals match, then **read every line top to bottom in plain words** and open the footnote on anything odd.

Then look for three pairs: debt due soon against cash, customer bills against cash, profit kept against cash.
cards.simpler: A real balance sheet is the same house photo with more rooms. Check that the three totals match. Then **read every line top to bottom in plain words**, and open the footnote on anything odd. Finally look for three pairs: debt due soon against cash, customer bills against cash, and profit kept against cash. Two years of columns show which way things are moving.

cards.body: Tonight: search any listed company's name plus 'annual report', open the PDF, find the balance sheet, and say its first 5 lines out loud in plain words. Then find cash and short-term borrowings. Which is bigger?
cards.simpler: Tonight, pick any company listed on a stock market. Search its name plus the words annual report and open the PDF. Find the balance sheet. Say its first five lines out loud in plain words. Then find two numbers: cash, and **short-term borrowings**, which means loans due within a year. Which one is bigger?

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now read a real published balance sheet from the totals down, say each line in plain words, and name any of the three warning signs it shows.
